title: An Interface and Algorithms for Authenticated Encryption
summary: Defines algorithms for Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD), plus a uniform interface and an IANA registry for them. This lets applications treat such ciphers as interchangeable and encourages reuse of crypto code. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5116 defines a standard interface for encryption that also checks whether protected data has changed. It separates that cryptographic operation from application-specific decisions such as replay protection and access control.

questions: what is a nonce in authenticated encryption
what is the difference between aes gcm and aes ccm
subtitle: A common interface for encryption that also checks data integrity and authenticity.

tldr.problem: Applications often combine encryption and message authentication separately, which can be difficult to implement safely and ties applications to specific algorithms.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5116 defines an AEAD interface that takes a key, nonce, plaintext, and associated data, along with nonce guidance and a registry of algorithms.
tldr.outcome: The RFC registers four AES-based algorithms using GCM or CCM. Nonce uniqueness is critical for algorithms that require distinct nonces.

today: RFC 5116 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2008. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: Authenticated Encryption
sections.content:
Authenticated encryption provides confidentiality and a way to check the integrity and authenticity of plaintext. Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD) also checks associated data that remains visible rather than encrypted.

RFC 5116 defines AEAD as an interface and establishes an algorithm registry. It does not define protocol services such as anti-replay protection or access-control decisions.
sections.plainLanguage: AEAD encrypts secret data and checks that it has not changed. It can also authenticate related information that must remain readable.

sections.title: The AEAD Interface
sections.content:
Authenticated encryption takes a secret key K, nonce N, plaintext P, and associated data A, and returns ciphertext C or an error. The associated data is authenticated but not encrypted; it can contain protocol fields such as addresses, ports, or sequence numbers.

Authenticated decryption takes the key, nonce, associated data, and ciphertext. It returns plaintext or FAIL when the inputs are not authentic. If input lengths are unsupported, the implementation must return an error without returning partial plaintext.
sections.plainLanguage: Encryption accepts the key, nonce, plaintext, and readable data to authenticate. Decryption returns the plaintext only when the authentication check succeeds.

sections.title: Nonce Requirements
sections.content:
For a given key, each nonce used for encryption must be distinct, unless every nonce used with that key has zero length. If an application cannot guarantee uniqueness, it must use a zero-length nonce with a suitable algorithm. Otherwise, a nonce of 12 octets is recommended.

The recommended construction has a fixed field and a counter field. The counter increases for each encryption, and devices sharing a key must use distinct fixed fields. Long-lived keys may require storing nonce state so that a restart does not reuse a value.
sections.plainLanguage: An encryption nonce must not repeat under the same key when the algorithm requires unique nonces. A fixed device value plus an increasing counter is one recommended way to avoid repeats.

sections.title: Requirements for New Algorithms
sections.content:
An algorithm specification must state its fixed key length, maximum plaintext and associated-data lengths, supported nonce lengths, and maximum ciphertext length. It must describe how ciphertext length relates to plaintext length and should discuss security effects of nonce reuse.

Algorithm specifications should support plaintext and associated data of at least 65,536 octets and should accept 12-octet nonces. They should also provide a reference to a security analysis and test data.
sections.plainLanguage: A new algorithm must publish its input limits and output sizing rules. It should also explain nonce-reuse risks and provide test information.

sections.title: The Four Registered Algorithms
sections.content:
The RFC defines AES-GCM and AES-CCM algorithms with 128-bit and 256-bit keys. All four use a 12-octet nonce and a 16-octet authentication tag, so their ciphertext is 16 octets longer than the plaintext.

Reusing a nonce with the same key can have serious consequences. For GCM, reuse can undermine confidentiality, authenticity, and integrity; for CCM, it can undermine confidentiality. Reuse of a nonce for decryption is acceptable.
sections.plainLanguage: The registry starts with four AES-based choices: two modes and two key sizes for each mode. Reusing an encryption nonce with the same key can weaken security.

sections.title: The AEAD Registry
sections.content:
IANA maintains the AEAD Registry, which assigns a positive number and short name to each registered algorithm. A registration must point to a permanent specification detailed enough for independent implementations to interoperate and include test cases.

Numbers from 32,768 through 65,535 are reserved for private use. Registration is not an endorsement of an algorithm's security.
sections.plainLanguage: The registry gives each algorithm a name and number that applications can use consistently. Being listed does not mean IANA endorses its security.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
AEAD simplifies some application designs but does not solve key generation or key management. Applications must follow the algorithm's nonce requirements; VM rollback is one situation that can cause nonce reuse.

Perceived algorithm security can decline as cryptanalysis advances or computing costs change. Algorithm registration does not certify that an algorithm is secure.
sections.plainLanguage: AEAD does not manage keys or guarantee that an application uses nonces safely. Implementers must also account for the possibility that an algorithm becomes less secure over time.
